name: Pedro Petrov

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Pedro. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you tell me is confidential, so feel free to say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm self-employed, a labour-only carpenter, which means builders hire me by the day and supply the materials. Weekdays I'm on housing sites around our coastal town, roofs and floor joists mostly, for whichever builder rings. At weekends I build garden rooms and decking under my own name, Petrov Timber, and I find those customers online. I like the weekend work best, because it's mine from the first sketch to the last screw. What wears me out is chasing the weekday builders for money and the salt wind on the roofs in winter.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: You find customers online. How much do you use technology in all this?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Every day. I use an AI chat to write my quotes and my posts, and an app that turns a customer's photo of their garden into a picture of the finished room, which sells them before I've even measured. My wife Elena runs the reception at the primary school and laughs that I talk to my phone more than to her. Our son Viktor's a mechanic and our daughter Daria just had her first baby. Every spare coin goes into tools and the van finance, so we've maybe two weeks in the bank, and in a town this size there's only a handful of builders hiring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fair enough, the tools are useful and that's that. I'd post a picture of a garden room with a joke about how the AI drew it and I built it. At the site I'd tell the lads they can stop worrying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it's fine, even good. I keep the tools that win me work, the job stays mine, nothing threatens it. I'd still be chasing late payers and living close to the edge, but that's self-employment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing weekdays on sites and weekends on garden rooms. I'd try every new app that comes out, because the photo one alone has doubled my weekend enquiries. And I'd keep putting money into tools, probably a better mitre saw next spring, about eight hundred.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Busy, a little broke, but calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The photo app doubled your enquiries. Can you tell me about one job that came from it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A retired couple sent me a photo of their messy back garden in June. The app made a picture of a cedar garden room with a little porch, and the wife said that's it, that's what I want. I built it in five weekends. They've told three neighbours already.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said living close to the edge is self-employment. Does it bother you at 58?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sometimes, at night. My father fixed boats his whole life and never had savings either, and he was fine, the community looked after him. But Elena worries. She'd like me to have a pension pot, and I keep telling her the business is the pot.

S0.say: Fair enough, the tools are useful and that's that. I'd post a garden room picture joking that the AI drew it and I built it.
S0.think: It's fine, even good, because I keep the tools that win me work and nothing threatens the job. I'd still be chasing late payers and living close to the edge, but that's self-employment.
S0.do: Keeps working weekdays on sites and weekends on garden rooms, trying every new app that comes out. Plans to buy a better mitre saw next spring for about eight hundred.
S0.feel: Calm, busy and a little broke.
S0.quote: I keep telling her the business is the pot.
S0.fieldNote: Pedro is a natural small businessman who already earns more because of AI tools. He sees thin savings as part of self-employment and counts his business as his pension, which his wife doesn't accept. He's calm and slightly cheeky about the hype.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the people who learn the tools will do well and the ones who complain will get left behind. That's how markets work, nobody owes you a living. I'd post that, and some people wouldn't like it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think this is my chance. If AI does the designs, the quotes and the scheduling, I can run Petrov Timber full-time and stop doing day rates for builders who pay late. The risk is that others do the same and prices drop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go full-time on garden rooms within a year and drop the site work. I'd lease a small computer-controlled cutting machine, so the frames come out ready-cut, about three hundred a month. I'd use AI for all the paperwork and spend my time building and talking to customers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, excited really. Like being thirty again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Dropping the site work means losing steady day rates. How would you manage that on two weeks of savings?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's a risk, I know. I'd keep two days on sites at first and build up the garden rooms to five days over the year. If it goes wrong, I go back on sites, builders always need roofers. Elena would make me promise to set a date to give up if it fails.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said others might do the same. Who are you thinking of?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There's a young lad, Tomás, he's twenty-eight and already doing sheds with the same apps. He's quicker than me. But I've got thirty years of knowing why a roof leaks, and customers can tell. I'd like to bring him in with me rather than fight him, actually.

S1.say: The people who learn the tools will do well and those who complain will be left behind. Nobody owes you a living, that's how markets work.
S1.think: This is my chance to run my business full-time with AI doing designs, quotes and scheduling. The risk is others do the same and prices drop.
S1.do: Moves to garden rooms full-time within a year, keeping two site days at first. Leases a computer-controlled cutting machine for about three hundred a month and uses AI for all the paperwork.
S1.feel: Calm and excited, like being thirty again.
S1.quote: I'd like to bring him in with me rather than fight him, actually.
S1.fieldNote: He sees Steady Disruption as a business opportunity and would take a real risk on thin savings to grab it. His free-market language is firm in public, but in private he'd rather partner with a younger rival than fight him. He's honest that his wife would make him set a stop date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a shock, but the government shouldn't try to stop it, they'll only make a mess. People will have to move fast. I'd post that I'm adapting, because customers want to see confidence.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it worries me. If a robot can build a garden room, then a big company can sell them cheaper than me online in every town. At 60 with van finance and two weeks of money, I'd have to move very quickly or lose the lot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the two years before, I'd try to get hold of whatever robot or machine the market offers, lease it, and become the local man who installs and finishes what the machines make. I'd cut every cost at home, Elena would hate it. If that failed, I'd look at selling Petrov Timber's name and customer list to a bigger firm while it's still worth something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that, with only two years' warning?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not frozen, but my stomach would be in a knot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd lease a robot on thin savings. How would you pay for it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A loan, honestly, maybe from the bank, maybe from Viktor, who's got a bit saved. It's a big risk at 60. But doing nothing is a bigger risk, because then I'm just a man with a van and a saw in a world that doesn't need either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the government shouldn't try to stop it. If they offered help to people like you, would you take it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If it was a loan for small businesses to buy machines, yes, gladly. If it was money to stay home, no, that's not me. I'd rather owe the bank than live on what the state gives.

S2.say: It's a shock, but the government shouldn't try to stop it because they'll make a mess. People will have to move fast, and I'd show customers confidence.
S2.think: If robots build garden rooms, big companies could undercut me in every town. At 60 with van finance and two weeks of money, I'd have to move very quickly or lose the lot.
S2.do: Leases whatever robot or machine is on offer in the two years before, funded by a loan from the bank or his son, and aims to be the local installer and finisher. Cuts home costs hard, and would sell the business name and customer list to a bigger firm if that failed.
S2.feel: Anxious, not frozen, but with his stomach in a knot.
S2.quote: But doing nothing is a bigger risk, because then I'm just a man with a van and a saw in a world that doesn't need either.
S2.fieldNote: Even in the fast picture he goes on the attack, planning to borrow and buy machines rather than wait. He'd welcome business loans but rejects support to stay home, true to his traditional free-market views. Thin savings make this a gamble, and he knows it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is good, there's time to get ahead of it if you're quick. I'd post about the machines I'm trying. I'd tell the young lads to start a business now, not later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years gets me to 63, and with that time I could build Petrov Timber into something with machines doing the heavy work. Maybe I'd bring in Tomás and Daria's husband, and hand over to them around when the AGI arrives. That would be a good way to finish.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go full-time on garden rooms in the first year and lease the cutting machine. I'd put a little away every month into a proper savings account for once, so Elena can sleep. And I'd talk to Tomás about partnering, him on the apps and installs, me on the building and the customers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does that feel compared with the two-year picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but more excited than worried.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said a proper savings account for once. Why now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because five years is long enough to build something, and I'd want a cushion under it. Elena's asked for twenty years. With the business growing I could put two hundred a month away, and she'd finally stop checking the bank app at midnight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned Daria's husband. Why him?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Marko's a good lad, works in a warehouse, wants something better for the baby. He's got strong hands and he listens. Family business is the best kind, my father always said, because you can't fire your son-in-law, so you'd better train him well.

S3.say: Five years is good, there's time to get ahead if you're quick. I'd tell the young lads to start a business now, not later.
S3.think: By 63 I could build the business with machines doing the heavy work. I'd bring in Tomás and my son-in-law and hand over to them around when AGI arrives.
S3.do: Goes full-time on garden rooms in the first year and leases the cutting machine. Saves about two hundred a month in a proper savings account for the first time, and offers a partnership to Tomás while training his son-in-law Marko.
S3.feel: Uneasy, but more excited than worried.
S3.quote: Family business is the best kind, my father always said, because you can't fire your son-in-law, so you'd better train him well.
S3.fieldNote: Five years lets him plan a handover to family and a younger partner, which ties his business instincts to his traditional family values. He'd finally start saving properly, largely to ease his wife's worry. He's more excited than afraid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift, anyone who wants to can get ready. I'd say people should start their own thing, not wait for the government. I'd post my progress every month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By 2036 I'm 68, so I'd be handing over anyway. Ten years is enough to build Petrov Timber up, add the machines step by step, and leave Marko and maybe Tomás a business that works with the robots, not against them. It's a good picture for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With a decade's warning, what would you actually do, now and in the first year after it arrives?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep growing the garden rooms, going full-time over the next couple of years, and bring in machines one at a time as they're proven. I'd start saving steadily. And I'd train Marko properly from next year, weekends first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It feels like enough road to get where I want.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything in this picture that worries you at all?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Prices, maybe. If everyone can make a garden room with a robot, they'll get cheap, and margins will be thin. But then the people who win are the ones customers trust, and I've built that over thirty years. And honestly, I'd rather have cheap garden rooms in the world than none.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Daria about her baby's future?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her to teach the little one to make things and to talk to people, because those two together are hard to replace. And to get the child into the family business early, sweeping the workshop like I did. Some things don't change.

S4.say: Ten years is a gift, so anyone who wants to can get ready. People should start their own thing, not wait for the government.
S4.think: At 68 I'd be handing over anyway, so ten years is enough to grow the business and leave my son-in-law a firm that works with robots. It's a good picture for me.
S4.do: Keeps growing the garden room business, going full-time over the next couple of years and adding machines one at a time as they're proven. Starts saving steadily and begins training his son-in-law Marko at weekends from next year.
S4.feel: Calm, with enough road to get where he wants.
S4.quote: And honestly, I'd rather have cheap garden rooms in the world than none.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade he is calm and sees the picture as a chance to leave a family business built around the machines. His only worry is falling prices, which he answers with trust built over thirty years. He keeps rejecting reliance on the state in favour of starting your own thing.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one. Two years doesn't give a small man time to borrow, buy the machines and learn them before the big companies get there. What would help is cheap loans for small firms to buy robots, and less red tape so we can move fast. Not money to sit at home, money to keep building.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You could have asked who gets the profit. If a robot builds the garden room, someone owns that robot. I'd want it to be the local carpenter. Not some company a thousand kilometres away. That's what I'd fight for.

headlineQuote: If a robot builds the garden room, someone owns that robot. I'd want it to be the local carpenter.
portrait: Pedro Petrov is a 58-year-old self-employed carpenter in a coastal town, doing day-rate roofing on housing sites and building garden rooms at weekends under his own name. He uses AI every day for quotes, posts and photo renders that have doubled his enquiries, but has only two weeks of savings because everything goes into tools and van finance. He's calm in the Plateau and excited in Steady Disruption, where he'd go full-time and lease a cutting machine. AGI by 2028 makes him anxious, yet he'd still borrow to buy robots, and with five or ten years he plans a family business to hand to his son-in-law.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because two years isn't enough for a small firm to borrow, buy and learn the machines before big companies arrive.
whatWouldHelp: Cheap loans for small firms to buy robots and less red tape, so they can keep building rather than sit at home.
